---
title: "Repeated units in linguistic data"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

The chapter on [independent sampling](../statistical-inference/independent-sampling.qmd) separated the number of recorded observations from the assumptions that make those observations independent. Linguistic experiments commonly contain repeated participants and items, so rows inherit dependence from the design.

We examine that structure in the **MALD connected-trial extract**. MALD is an auditory lexical-decision database described by Tucker et al. ([2019](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1056-1)); the later [MALD 1.1 release](https://doi.org/10.7939/r3-kh0r-r116) expanded the participant inventory. The paper reports 231 listeners, whereas release 1.1 contains 440. These totals describe different versions and should not be combined.

## Examining repetition in the MALD table

The prepared extract is response-blind: participants and words were selected without using correctness or response time. It is not the full release. One row records one real-word trial from one participant, including the spoken word, response time, correctness, SUBTLEX frequency, acoustic duration, and within-run trial order.

```{r}
#| label: mald-structure
mald_all <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald_all, correct == 1L)

participant_counts <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ participant_id,
  data = mald,
  FUN = length
)
item_counts <- aggregate(
  log_rt ~ item,
  data = mald,
  FUN = length
)

structure_summary <- c(
  connected_rows = nrow(mald_all),
  correct_latency_rows = nrow(mald),
  participants = length(unique(mald$participant_id)),
  word_items = length(unique(mald$item)),
  participant_word_pairs = nrow(unique(mald[c("participant_id", "item")]))
)
structure_summary
```

The latency analysis retains correct responses, as in Tucker et al.'s source analysis. This restriction leaves `r format(nrow(mald), big.mark = ",")` trials from `r length(unique(mald$participant_id))` participants and `r format(length(unique(mald$item)), big.mark = ",")` spoken words. It does not make the retained rows independent.

```{r}
#| label: plot-mald-repetition
library(ggplot2)

repetition_data <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    unit = "Participant",
    repetitions = participant_counts$log_rt
  ),
  data.frame(
    unit = "Word item",
    repetitions = item_counts$log_rt
  )
)

ggplot(repetition_data, aes(x = repetitions)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey55", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~unit, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Correct trials per unit", y = "Units") +
  theme_classic()
```

The two panels show different replication structures. A participant contributes many lexical decisions, while a word is heard by more than one participant. Thus the trial count, participant count, and item count answer different questions.

## Writing the independence claim

A regression model without grouping terms often represents conditional independence as

$$
f(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\prod_i f(y_i\mid\mathbf x_i,\boldsymbol\beta).
$$

After the predictors are known, the joint density is written as a product over trials. Under this model, learning the residual for one row gives no information about the residual for another.

That claim is implausible here for two distinct reasons. Responses from one participant may resemble each other because that listener has a persistent response-speed baseline. Responses to one word may resemble each other because its acoustic and lexical properties are not completely represented by the measured predictors. Observing one trial can thus change what we expect for another trial that shares its participant or word.

## Distinguishing crossed and nested units

Participant and word are **crossed** because participants respond to many words and words receive responses from multiple participants. A nested structure would instead require each lower-level unit to belong to only one higher-level unit. For instance, runs belong to participant sessions in the MALD release; a run identifier does not migrate between participants.

The distinction can be checked from the incidence table rather than inferred from column order:

```{r}
#| label: mald-crossing-check
crossing_check <- c(
  smallest_participant_item_inventory = min(participant_counts$log_rt),
  largest_participant_item_inventory = max(participant_counts$log_rt),
  smallest_item_listener_inventory = min(item_counts$log_rt),
  largest_item_listener_inventory = max(item_counts$log_rt)
)
crossing_check
```

## Matching dependence to the claim

A participant-population claim requires replication across participants. An item-population claim requires replication across words. A claim about both requires a design and analysis that preserve both sources. More trials from the same participants or words improve estimates for those units but do not add participant or word replication.

Averaging trials within participants would preserve participant replication while discarding word variation and within-participant trial predictors. Averaging within words would do the reverse. Mixed-effects models retain trial-level responses while representing both shared sources.

Before fitting one, record four facts: (i) what one response row represents, (ii) which sampled units recur, (iii) whether those units are crossed or nested, and (iv) the populations across which the linguistic association should generalize. The [next page](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) translates those design facts into population coefficients and group distributions.
